name: Nasal splint after rhinoplasty

card.summary: A rigid or semi-rigid cover, sometimes with internal stents, that holds the reshaped nose still while it heals.
card.aka: External nasal splint, thermoplastic splint, internal nasal splint
card.note: Worn only during early healing and placed by the surgical team; studies of splints and packing are mostly in septal and nasal surgery.

quick.overview:
After rhinoplasty the nose is typically taped and covered with a splint so the newly reshaped bones and cartilage do not move while the incisions heal. Surgeons often remove the dressing about a week later.

Splints also exist inside the nose, for example silastic or resorbable types used after septal surgery or in cleft nose repair. The research on them is mixed in scope and mostly about complications and comfort.
quick.mechanism: The splint immobilises and protects the tissues, shielding the surgical result from pressure and knocks during early healing. Internal splints support the septum or cartilage from inside.
quick.risks: Reported issues in the literature include discomfort, bacterial colonization with internal splints and, in one study, respiratory distress with totally occlusive packing compared with splints or sutures. Percutaneous osteotomy scars have also been described in rhinoplasty.

lead: A nasal splint is a protective device placed over or inside the nose after surgery. After rhinoplasty, the surgeon typically applies tape and a custom-shaped splint to keep the nose still while the incisions and bones heal, and the dressing is removed about one week after the procedure [1]. The splint helps the surgical result by holding the reshaped nasal bones and cartilage in their new position, shielding the nose from knocks, and in some designs applying light pressure to reduce swelling and bruising around the eyes [11][12].

Internal splints and nasal packing are used in septal and nasal surgery, and studies have compared them with transseptal sutures and with no packing in terms of bleeding, comfort and complications [2][3][4]. Materials have included silastic sheets, rapidly setting conformable external splint material, thermoplastic and 3D-printed custom splints, and resorbable internal splints [5][6][7][12][15].
Surgeons differ on how essential external splinting is: a systematic review found few studies on it, and a plastic surgery case series asked whether it is needed at all [11][15].
infobox: Placed at the end of surgery; external dressing removed about one week later [1]
Hold nasal bones and cartilage in position, protect, limit swelling [11]

paras: In a rhinoplasty, the nose is prepared with paper tape and then covered by a shaped splint to protect tender tissues; a stent inside the nose may also be used [1]. A survey of facial plastic surgeons examined practice patterns in the perioperative care of septorhinoplasty patients, indicating that splinting practices vary between surgeons [8].

Specialised splints have been described for particular problems, such as a dynamic nostril splint used in nasal tip surgery in cleft patients and a resorbable internal splint used in unilateral cleft lip nasal repair to shield the alar cartilage from scar forces [7][9].

An external splint is usually a moulded thermoplastic or metal piece taped over the nasal dorsum, while an internal splint is a thin silastic or resorbable sheet placed against the septum. A French group described a customised thermoplastic splint moulded to the new nose and worn for several weeks to guide scarring, in 43 patients over two years [13]. A 1947 paper in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery described yet another external splint, showing the device has a long history in nasal surgery [17].

A randomised trial in 95 patients examined packing types and a silastic splint after routine nasal surgery [2]. In a comparison of 150 septoplasty patients, totally occlusive nasal packing was associated with an increased risk of respiratory distress during recovery from anesthesia compared with internal splints and transseptal sutures [3]. Another study looked at the timing of internal splint use with respect to bacterial colonization, complications and patient discomfort [10].

Rhinoplasty often includes osteotomies, in which the nasal bones are intentionally fractured and moved inward to narrow a wide nasal base. A splint holds those segments in place while they set [14]. Surgeons also say that the splint spreads gentle pressure that limits swelling, which matters because swelling can take months to resolve and the final shape of the nose only appears once it settles; Wikipedia notes that swelling can take at least a year to fully resolve [1].

A 2021 randomised trial of 40 open-rhinoplasty patients compared a traditional thermoplastic splint with a 3D-printed custom splint designed to press on the lateral osteotomy lines and nearby periorbital area; scores for bruising and swelling were lower in the custom-splint group across follow-up, with significant differences in ecchymosis at most time points between 1 hour and 15 days [12]. A 2015 randomised trial in about 40 patients compared a splint that extended beyond the osteotomy lines with one trimmed above them, with outcomes including satisfaction with dorsal aesthetic lines, brow lines and osteotomy lines at 12 months [14].

Trials and comparative studies have examined nasal packs, internal splints and transseptal sutures after septal surgery [2][3][4][10], a prospective study evaluated a conformable, rapidly setting splint material [5], and a survey described practice patterns among facial plastic surgeons [8].

On external splints specifically, a 2023 systematic review searching Cochrane, Medline and Embase identified 1,617 articles and included four studies published between 2016 and 2021 covering 2,425 patients, only 20 of whom used external splints; among 2,415 who did not, 151 had moderate periorbital oedema and ecchymosis and 99 percent showed a decrease in nasal width [11]. A 2019 report asked whether external splinting is a must and described a study of cosmetic results in its absence [15]. The randomised comparisons of custom 3D-printed and trimmed splints are described above [12][14].

A 2026 randomised trial of 200 rhinoplasty patients tested whether a decorative evil-eye bead on the splint changed the patient's perception of the new nose; participants said they were pleased to have one even when they did not describe themselves as believers [18].

Splints appear in recovery diaries and surgery-planning discussions as the visible sign of a nose job: the first week with tape and a splint, the removal appointment, and then months of swelling before the result is judged. Surgeons and patients in the research literature treat the splint as part of the healing process rather than a cosmetic accessory, although the study of an evil-eye bead on the splint shows some patients personalise it [18].
